observed_mechanics: 0x00bbaa60/0x00bbaa75 PUSH/POP ESI is the only frame work; the function has no locals and cannot spill.

0x00bbaa63 CALL 0x00bba640 is issued before anything is read, and its return value is never consumed. 0x00bbaa68 then re-reads the vector base, so the callee is a lazy-populate step that can reallocate and whose effect the caller must observe through the field, not through EAX.

0x00bbaa640's live body is 116 instructions ending in a bare RET; it compares ((this+0x88)-(this+0x84))>>2 against the zero-extended byte at +0x0ac and returns immediately when they are equal, so the sync is idempotent and costs nothing once the vector is the right size.

When the sizes differ, 0x00bba640 calls 0x00e25bd0 to clear the vector, then loops mPlanetCount times; per iteration it forms a StarID by adding i*0x1000000 to the dword at +0x70, builds a four-word request {star_id, 0x5220cb8, 1, 0}, calls 0x0067dcd0 and then the game-mode manager's vtable slot +0x0c, and type-checks the result against 0x3e434e1 through vtable slot +0xc before appending it.
0x00bbaa68 reads only the begin pointer at +0x84; the end and capacity at +0x88 and +0x8c are not read here, so the function has no way to know the vector's size.
0x00bbaa6e MOV ECX,[ESP+0x8] loads the index as a full 32-bit dword with no sign extension, truncation to 16 or 32 bits, or masking.

0x00bbaa72 MOV EAX,[EAX+ECX*0x4] is the only bounds-relevant instruction in the body and there is no compare against the end pointer anywhere, so an out-of-range index is an unchecked read. This is a real invariant of the observed code, not an omission in the reconstruction.
0x00bbaa76 RET 0x4 pops the index word, so a caller may pass the argument in a register or push it and leave the stack to the callee; either spelling is consistent with the observed bytes.
0x00bbaa60 appears nowhere in .rdata or .data as a dword (scan total=0), so it is a non-virtual member and its class is not vtable-proven.

callees_evidence.identified_operation: lazy planet-vector synchronisation. Guard: if ((end-begin)>>2) == (uint8)mPlanetCount, return. Otherwise clear the vector through 0x00e25bd0 and, mPlanetCount times, derive a StarID from the dword at +0x70 plus i*0x1000000, build the request {star_id, 0x5220cb8, 1, 0}, invoke the game-mode manager, type-check the result against cPlanetRecord::TYPE 0x3e434e1, addref it through vtable slot 0 and append it, growing through 0x00aea5d0 when the capacity is exhausted, then release the transient holder through vtable slot +0x04.

semantic_contract: Given a star record, this function returns the planet record at a given orbit index, materialising the record's planet list on first use. 1. It calls 0x00bba640 on the receiver with no arguments and discards the result (0x00bbaa63). That port is idempotent: it returns immediately when the receiver's planet vector already holds exactly as many elements as the receiver's mPlanetCount byte, and otherwise clears and rebuilds the vector. 2. Only after that does it read the vector's begin pointer from the receiver at +0x84 (0x00bbaa68), so a reallocation performed by step 1 is observed. 3. It loads the index from its single stack argument as a full 32-bit value with no masking or sign extension, and returns vector[index] (0x00bbaa6e, 0x00bbaa72). Invariants: the function never writes to the receiver itself; the index is completely unchecked, since the end pointer at +0x88 is never read here, so an index outside the populated range is an out-of-bounds read; the callee owns the cleanup of the one stack word, proven by RET 0x4; and the whole observable result depends on the sync port having run first, which is why the two functions must not be separated.
classification_rationale: The complete 25-byte body, the ABI including the callee-popped argument, the single field offset, the constants, the single direct callee and the absence of any branch were all read from the disassembly, and the callee was disassembled in full plus decompiled so the lazy-load contract is established rather than assumed. The one fully inspected caller confirms the receiver is a star record and the argument is an orbit index. It is not STRONG_SEMANTIC because: (a) OWNING CLASS AND METHOD NAME - the function is non-virtual and appears in no vtable, so cStarRecord and GetPlanetRecord are candidates resting on five offset agreements and one SDK declaration, not on vtable proof; (b) the bounds contract of the index is not merely unknown, it is absent: nothing in the function or its callee validates it, so the reconstruction cannot state what a caller must guarantee; (c) the sync port's per-iteration request literal 0x5220cb8 and the meaning of advancing the StarID by 0x1000000 per element are unestablished, so the population rule is known mechanically but not semantically; and (d) only one of the 20 canonical callers was disassembled, and it passes the literal index 0, so the general orbit-index contract rests on a single narrow observation.
semantic_findings: The function is a lazy accessor with an explicit load step, and the load is ordered before the field read on purpose: re-reading the base pointer after the call is what makes a reallocating load safe.

The index is used raw. There is no compare against the vector's end pointer anywhere in the function or in the sync port, so the out-of-range case is undefined behaviour in the original, not an error return.
The sync port is idempotent and cheap when already populated, so the accessor is cheap in steady state and expensive only on the first call after the planet list is invalidated.

The sync port's per-iteration StarID arithmetic adds 0x1000000 to the base id, which with Spore-ModAPI's StarID packing advances the sector field; that is why one star's record can hold planets belonging to more than one sector index, and it is a load-bearing detail of the population rule rather than a loop counter.

The sync port type-checks each fetched object against cPlanetRecord::TYPE (0x3e434e1) through a vtable call, so a null or wrong-typed fetch is skipped rather than appended; the vector therefore only ever contains cPlanetRecord pointers.
The Ghidra decompilation of this function is faithful here (unlike its sibling at 0x00c472e0): the argument order and the discard of the callee's result are both correct in the pseudocode.
unresolved_questions: Which class and method is this, strictly? The evidence supports cStarRecord::GetPlanetRecord(size_t), but the SDK gives no address for that declaration and the function is in no vtable.

What are the valid index bounds, and who guarantees them? Nothing here checks, so the contract is entirely on the callers; the 19 other canonical callers were not disassembled and might not all be well-behaved.
What does the literal 0x5220cb8 in the per-iteration request mean? It has no SDK name and appears as a constant in the request word adjacent to the StarID.

Why does the sync advance the StarID by 0x1000000 per element instead of populating from a list? mPlanetCount is a plain byte with no accompanying table of ids in the object, so the ids must be derived. The derivation rule is observed but its intent is not.

Is 0x00bbaa60 ever called with the intent to trigger the load only, ignoring the result? The 20 canonical callers include several whose names suggest other subsystems, and none of the uninspected ones was checked for result use.

What is 0x00bba900 really? The SDK calls it GetPlanetRecords but the body is a boolean predicate over mPlanetCount and mFlags bit 12, and its JNZ leaves the function. Left unclassified; resolving it would sharpen the naming of this whole cluster.
runtime_gates: No original-process trace exists for 0x00bbaa60; every claim is static.

A runtime trace would be needed to observe the actual StarIDs the sync requests, to confirm that the vector is repopulated rather than merely reallocated on the second call, and to see whether any caller ever passes an out-of-range index.
The runtime value of mPlanetCount and of the vector's capacity for a real star is not recoverable statically.
